Philippa Long and Georgia Lepper

Georgia Lepper

[Philippalong@uwclub.net]

Georgia Lepper  

psychoanalytic psychotherapy, metaphor, research, single case studies, mentalization

Twelve transcripts, three from each of four patients, taken from the early, mid and late phases of open-ended, long-term psychoanalytic psychotherapy with the same therapist, were analysed for metaphor. Metaphors were categorized into key, novel and conventional. Using grounded theory metaphors were categorized by theme and function. It was found that all metaphors - novel, conventional and key - could be representative of key concepts such as the self, others/relationships and therapy/self transformation and diagnosis or psychopathology; chart change; indicate mentalization (Fonagy et al. 2004). In addition use of metaphors by different patients showed different patterns that co-occurred with good or bad outcome.

Gertrud Mander

Gertrud Mander  

Patrick Casement's first book, On Learning from the Patient, was a bestseller when it was published 20 years ago and it soon became required reading throughout the profession. The present book is his fourth book, after Further Learning from the Patient and Learning from Our Mistakes. I am strongly tempted to connect this Learning from ‥. series with Bion's Learning from Experience (1962), which was a difficult disquisition about significant learning and dealing with anxiety in which many of Casement's ideas originate. He has developed his own didactic and narrative style, demonstrating with the use of plentiful clinical material how he works, thinks and achieves therapeutic results with his patients and thereby instructs his readers how to learn. In the present autobiographical account he relates his personal experiences from difficult beginnings through becoming a social worker to training as a psychoanalyst, once again repeating the successful formula that has made his books so readable for trainees, clinical practitioners and interested lay readers. Part story-telling, part detailed explanation of his shrewdly interpretative methodology, he describes the analytic dialogue as an ingenious strategy to communicate with patients, learning from them and understanding his therapeutic influence on them, but also registering his countertransference and constantly monitoring his mistakes.

[[RunningHead]]

Childe Roland and the Mystic's Quest: Analytic Faith in a World of Lost Meanings

Christopher MacKenna

Christopher MacKenna

37 Clifden Road, Worminghall, Bucks HP18 9JR. [cmackenna@stmarylebone.org]

Christopher MacKenna  

faith, knowledge, meaning, unknowing, evenly hovering, Browning

Psychoanalysis did not emerge in a vacuum. With hindsight, we can see that it was - at least in part - a response to a dual crisis in the Northern European world at the end of the nineteenth century: a crisis of religious faith, and a crisis about knowledge and the possibility of meaning. With help from Henry Scott Holland and Robert Browning, this paper seeks to evoke these crises, and then to explore the way in which Freud's psychoanalysis, based on the practice of ‘evenly hovering attention’, introduced a secularized world to the practice of ‘unknowing’ which had previously been the preserve of the mystics. Similarities between the work of analysis and the mystical quest are explored, and it is suggested that both are forms of knowing, in which meaning is able to emerge through a process of mutual participation in being.

The Challenge of Working with Staff Groups in the Caring Professions: The Importance of the ‘Team Development and Reflective Practice Group’

Bill Thorndycraft and Jennifer Mccabe

Jennifer Mccabe

90 Court Way, Twickenham, Middx TW2 7SW. [billthorndycraft@hotmail.com]

30 Borough High Street, London SE1 1XU. [jenniferamccabe@aol.com]

Jennifer Mccabe  

boundaries, staff groups, borderline personality disorder, mental health, consumerism

This paper highlights the importance of providing a regular space for teams of professionals, working in the mental health field and caring professions, to reflect on how the work impacts on the team dynamics and their own mental health. It explores the role of the group facilitator and how that role differs from working with patient and other groups. It considers the context of the current political environment within which mental health services operate and explores how this may impact on individual and team ego strength, leading to regression and reliance on primitive defence mechanisms as a means to coping and survival. Also considered is the issue of the challenges presented in working with teams where traits and features consistent with borderline personality disorder (DSM-4 Cluster B) manifest in the team. The authors propose a model called ‘Team Development and Reflective Practice Groups’, and suggest guidelines for providing an optimum facilitating environment for the professionals within these groups.

Isabel Menzies Lyth 1917-2008

Jean Neumann PHD

Jean Neumann

Jean Neumann   Director of Studies and Core Faculty, Advanced Organisational Change, and Consulting Programme, The Tavistock Institute, London

When Isabel Menzies Lyth retired from her various roles at the Tavistock Institute, I remember the loss of her edgy, wise presence. She had been recruited onto the Institute's Council at a time when the main strategic debates were coalescing around social policy research versus action research and consulting. She was as likely to come down on the side of economics and capability as she was to argue in favour of a sensible approach to human resources management.

I cannot claim to have known Isabel well, but I am certain that she is ‘inside’ me as an archetype: a true elder of the Tavistock Institute's traditions internalized as the image of woman action researcher ageing deeply. For me, she combined a commitment both to psychoanalysis and to organizational analysis. I wonder where the Institute would be today if Isabel's health hadn't forced her to withdraw from Council and its committees. It did take us a decade to reclaim our action research and consulting heritage.

In teaching consultants and change managers, I still use her story of how the nurses didn't like her ‘mechanisms of defence’ paper. Isabel, herself, seemed unable to accept the full scientific influence of that work precisely because the difficulties of helping the client system work with the ideas remained very much in her memory. Elliot Jacques once told me that he thought Isabel's version of social defences was much more seminal than his own paper on the topic. Happily, the two well-respected volumes of essays she produced from ‘retirement’ (Menzies Lyth 1988, 1989) recorded her scholarly practice at the Tavistock Institute, clearly much broader than credited previously.

Dr Jean E. Neumann PhD

Editorial

Gertrud Mander and Linda Pethick

Linda Pethick

[g.mander@virgin.net]

[linda@bpethick.freeserve.co.uk]

Linda Pethick  

This issue contains a rich mixture of papers, beginning with this year's BJP Lecture, ‘Pluralism in contemporary psychoanalysis: theory and practice’ by Jean White, who explores pluralism as a clinical tool, in the sense of Bion's ‘multiple vertices’, and stresses the many perspectives nowadays available to the clinician in the wake of the paradigm shifts in the profession which the models developed by Winnicott, Lacan, Ogden, Jessica Benjamin and others set in train. White maintains that it is important for the contemporary clinician to acquire and foster a capacity to hold different perspectives in mind while working with patients. In support of her claim, she quotes Bollas who advises the clinician to use different responses with different patients and stresses the centrality of the capacity to recognize and metabolize difference for psychic growth to take place. With the aid of interesting clinical material White demonstrates that we are in urgent need of developing an attitude of active pluralism, and that we should encourage and practise in-depth discussions of the principles underlying the main theoretical standpoints governing contemporary psychoanalysis.

Following this theoretical investigation, David Morgan's more clinical paper, ‘Enactment: moving from deadly ways of relating to the beginnings of mental life’, explores the need for the borderline and psychotic patient to experience the analyst's struggle with the very real experiences being projected into him. By using clinical material from two patients dominated by monolithic thinking, who employed actions for evacuating their feelings of discomfort (one through enuresis, the other through violence and perversion), Morgan demonstrates the importance for the analyst of bearing his feelings of discomfort at a physical and emotional level. He showed how in time he was able to actively symbolize them in ways which eventually allowed the patients to move from their powerful concrete thinking and enactment to the beginnings of thinking for themselves.

Barry Proner  

The author sets out to question the practice by many analysts of routinely seeing patients five times a week for fifty minutes. He is understandably moved to reflect on this when his experience is that, in the matters of time and frequency, no discussion is possible and his colleagues work in that way because that is how they ‘like to work’ and because that is how their own analysts worked.

208

He makes what would seem to be a valid plea for the analyst to recognize the problem with the routine practice of favouring four to five times-weekly treatment no matter how suitable the work is for the patient. His concerns are for patients who clearly use such analysis for purposes other than emotional growth (what I would call addictive use) such as ‘having a reliable person they can talk to’.

He is occupied at one level with the ethics of the psychoanalyst who might take advantage of a patient's dependency, greed or naïvety. The author seems to favour strictures in order to control the analyst's unconscious or conscious greed or excess of zeal in addition to unquestioning adherence to an inherited form, assuming that analysts can lack the integrity and judgement to determine the most effective way of working with their patient. This is understandable if, as he says it is his experience, his colleagues apply a universal approach ‘because that is how I like to work’, a Procrustean, one-size-fits-all ‘technique’.

Naturally the patient's life circumstances - the reality of external reality, as it were - must be understood. The example of an analyst who saw his patient's failure to attend the fifth session as ‘resistance’ when there were real external circumstances is also a caricature, an analyst who can see only internal reality, yet the analyst may not have been entirely incorrect either. As an analyst, would he have been doing his job if he had not thought from many angles about the reasons for his patient refusing a fifth session? It is the analyst's responsibility to reflect deeply on the matters of the frequency as well as the length of sessions with each patient. The issue of how and when to propose an increase or perhaps a decrease in the frequency is part of that responsibility.

This paper contains a set of thoughtful observations, drawn from many years of experience in psychoanalytic psychotherapy, on the question of how many sessions a week analysts choose to offer their patients and why, with a whole set of connected factors related to this issue.

As the paper makes observations designed to engage in this debate, but does not construct a hypothesis, argue for and against this, through presenting findings, and then drawing a set of conclusions, it is difficult not to find points of agreement and disagreement with what is said, but in a somewhat arbitrary fashion. So much of what is said makes useful and good sense, in a general way.

I noted that the author says that his communication comes from ‘personal work experience’, which includes ‘personal belief’, ‘idiosyncratic choice’ and ‘faith’ and he has a level of scepticism about ‘sophisticated language’ that ‘supposedly characterizes a scientific pronouncement’. Nevertheless, the demonstration and attempted evaluation of our psychoanalytically informed postulates, theoretical and technical, need to take place. This is done through the written dissemination of our work in professional journals and books, through shared formal discussion and debate, and through the establishment of educational models of training for candidates derived from this. In spite of the difficulty of supplying proof, rather than amassing evidence that can be scrutinized, we continue to demonstrate, and attempt to evaluate, our work. We therefore have to allow for the central paradox of ‘not knowing’, but ‘knowing in part’ to reside at the core of psychoanalytic practice. We certainly do have to try to find better and better ways to address what is so difficult to address formally. Therefore, defining the parameters of what we can usefully describe, for the purposes of enhancing understanding, applies, as much as ever, in this instance of the formulation of a paper that tackles the question of the provision of time to analytic patients.

Penny Wigram

London
[pa@wigram.org]

Penny Wigram  

What is it that draws the experienced therapist to yet another book on psychological therapy? The need for research perhaps, or curiosity about the work of a colleague? For me it has to contain material that will make me think, agree and disagree, and evoke reflections on concepts and ideas that will inform and refresh my own work with patients.

All this is offered to us in abundance in these collected papers and essays by Gertrud Mander. She says herself that there is no connecting theme to her writings over a period of 25 years but I would disagree. The theme is that we are invited to share the thoughts and interests of a generous and erudite writer who is willing to let the reader into the world of the therapist while keeping her totally professional stance at all times.

The collection of papers is divided into two sections - Part 1, ‘Models and Methods’, and Part 2, ‘Clinical and Other Matters’. Gertrud Mander declares herself to be a practitioner, in the main, of once-weekly and short-term therapy. In the first part of the book she gives us essays arguing the benefits of these forms of therapy. I found this part of the book difficult in some ways as it differs from my preferred way of working. However, what Mander does not take into conscious account is that, although she may work short-term and once weekly, her work is based on a foundation of a broad knowledge of psychoanalytic theory and extensive reading of the great thinkers since Freud who have informed our long-term work. In her writing she shares with us her considerable knowledge and references to a broad spectrum of psychoanalytic theory and to literature.

In light of this, my question would be whether the more recent practitioners of short-term work are obliged to have had their own therapy in order to practise, or are required to embark on anything approximate to the studying and research that have gone into the writings in this book.

The first paper begins by introducing Mander's reflections on the importance of endings. In a way, all analysis is interminable. Psychodynamic therapy begins an internal process in the patient that never ends, but she reminds us that the Woody Allen experience of 40 years in therapy is no longer appropriate or therapeutic. We are reminded that it was normal for Freud to work for two years only with his patients, albeit at five or six sessions a week.

Jan Hepburn  

My response to this paper is in two parts; some of my thoughts on the paper, and some of my thoughts about the question it poses. I do disagree with some of the paper's assertions and implications. The author outlines the various strands of thought he has had about this question, and suggests that as a profession we are not careful enough with what the question to increase brings forth about the patient and the treatment. I felt that the paper has a rather admonishing tone at times, and found myself wondering who the author has in mind. I believe that very few psychotherapists/psychoanalysts are as rigid as he describes, and I take a different view. I think he is implying that the views that psychotherapists hold about frequency are more akin to shibboleths - fixed and often outmoded doctrines which have to be adhered to rather than thought about. I see them more as fixed points of the compass the therapist uses to orient him/herself in order to have some framework; I do not believe this necessarily means that they are not thought about, or are not amenable to change. I am also not entirely clear what the author is saying about the value of psychoanalytic psychotherapy, and whether in fact he thinks it useful and appropriate in only a few cases.

There is a direct assertion in the paper which I did not agree with:

There is general agreement that psychotic patients have a poor prognosis when considered for psychodynamic therapy. The same applies to others presenting serious psychological disturbances (e.g. Asperger's syndrome, addictions, manic-depressive illness, personality disorders, etc.) and yet we can find that some of these patients may be quite keen to embark on psychodynamic therapy and may often want to continue having it for extremely long periods of time. I believe that even when both patient and therapist are happy with the progress of the work, i.e. there is improvement in some areas of the patient's life, the prognosis for change of the basic pathology is very doubtful. It is always wise to consider therapy with these patients as being of an experimental nature.

Ricardo Stramer

London

Ricardo Stramer  

This book is written with the interest and motivation of the historical scientist. By illuminating the disagreements and dissensions between Stekel and Freud, the authors contend that marginalization is symptomatic of large group processes and is a necessary process enabling a system of ideas to evolve. Bos and Groenendijk contend that, in order to look at why a person becomes marginalized, the researcher has to look at the dialogical discourse, that is, the latent content of the unconscious forces that create the dynamics between the players involved in the marginalization process.

The method the authors employ to study this phenomenon is based on the model inspired by the post-structuralist approach as exemplified by Michel Foucault, Jacques Derrida et al., which points out the importance of the unconscious aspects of culture in its manifestations through the discourse and the text in which it is inscribed. In order to achieve this task, the authors examine three main elements: the socio-ideological dimension of marginalization; the phenomenon of self-marginalization by one of the early participants of the psychoanalytical movement, Wilhelm Stekel, and, finally, the role played by Sigmund Freud in the marginalizing process.

Wilhelm Stekel was a physician and first came to Freud for a short stint of analysis (eight sessions) for his sexual problems, including impotence and excessive masturbation. He soon became a close collaborator and in 1902 founded the weekly discussion group which later became the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society, which included analysts such as Alfred Adler, Paul Federn, Otto Rank, amongst others. In 1910 Freud appointed Stekel and Adler co-editors of the first journal of psychoanalysis, the Zentralblatt. However, the disagreements and tensions between Stekel and Freud continued to grow and in 1912 Stekel officially withdrew from the Vienna Society. In 1938 Stekel fled from Germany to the UK, where he died in 1940.

He was a prolific writer and published around 367 works amongst which are the ten-volume work, Disorders of Instincts and Emotions (1921), and The Language of Dreams: An Exposition on Symbolism and Interpretation of Dreams in Relation to Mental Health and Illness (1911)

This book is the ninth in the series. More are projected.

While I can see that it is a worthwhile venture to put groups of International Journal of Psychoanalysis papers, classified under themes, into book form, I think it has its drawbacks. The more casual shopper might seize on this volume and, once home with it, be disappointed to realize that s/he has already read every word. Arguably, s/he should have spotted the Journal's name written clearly at the bottom of the front cover; but s/he might not have. As an ageing profession, many of us probably have several decades-worth of this valued periodical on our shelves, and our memories may not yet have atrophied.

That makes it more surprising, at least to me, that all the papers selected for this volume are less than ten years old. The IJP, I learn from the Series Preface, is now aged 80.I would have been very glad if the first 50 years of its life had been quarried and represented. I would then have seen papers that have never been in my possession in the form in which they were originally published. But in fact the first 72 years of the Journal's life are ignored in this selection. Why?

It occurs to me that the use of literature in psychoanalytic writing may not be new, but is on the increase. As a profession, we are now much more sensitive to matters of confidentiality - not before time - than our predecessors were.

Monica Lanyado PHD

Monica Lanyado

Monica Lanyado   Child and Adolescent Psychotherapist, Association of Child, Psychotherapists

Having read and been fascinated by Isabel's seminal work in organizations, plus having been on a ‘mini-Leicester’ conference in which she was a highly enigmatic staff member, I had never dreamt that I would have

527

supervision with this rather formidable lady. Isabel, by now in her eighties, agreed to my visiting her in Oxford once a month, for a morning's supervision on my consultation work with the staff of small organizations working with severely deprived children. There was a period when she offered to read the book on which I was working (Lanyado 2003), when the morning extended through lunch and into the afternoon. I would leave, reeling from all the interesting and always challenging discussion. Isabel would be merely a ‘wee bit tired’!

My fond memories are accompanied with gratitude for all that Isabel contributed to the understanding and environmental care of ill and severely deprived children, which was expressed in her many years of consultation to the staff of the Cotswold Community. Isabel's writings enable some sense to be made of the enormous difficulties and strains faced by staff trying to offer therapeutic help of many kinds, to children who are looked after by the local authorities. No doubt, Isabel's analysis with Bion and her lifelong appreciation of how mad big groups can become, particularly if they are working with ‘mad’ people, made her highly aware of how readily organizations can lose sight of their core task and end up crazy and unhealthy places to work in, or to be ‘looked after’ by.

Isabel remained committed to the value of working with children, to the end. She also remained deeply identified with her Scottish roots. She must have thought long and hard about asking those who wished to remember her to send donations to the Scottish Child Psychotherapy Trust, rather than sending flowers to her funeral. In this way she truly honoured our profession.

Dr Monica Lanyado PhD

Peter Agulnik FRCPsych

Peter Agulnik

Oxford

Peter Agulnik  

My first encounter with Isabel was in phantasy! I was in analysis with Oliver Lyth, and not knowing he was a widower, his ‘spouse’ was subject to intense scrutiny. There was a transformation to a more reality-focused transference when, in 1975, Oliver uprooted from North Oxford to a lovely Georgian house in Iffley, complete with this wife of formidable reputation. Following Oliver's death in 1981 I introduced myself. Somewhat to my relief, she said she knew who I was, and readily agreed to discuss how she might make a contribution to the McKnight Unit, a ward for people with severe and enduring psychoses at Littlemore Hospital, for which I held consultant psychiatric responsibility.

Littlemore was strongly involved in the Therapeutic Community approach and there was a culture of group work and staff support. Isabel encouraged a vigorous examination of role and practice, and my suggestion was that Isabel be invited to be a consultant to the weekly staff meeting. The introduction of this new style of group emphasized thinking about individual and corporate task and role to help the ward function in an optimal way. It was obligatory for all staff members, including domestic staff, to attend the group, so that ambivalence and resistance were ubiquitous. Nevertheless, the group survived, and continued for many years, even after Isabel retired, and new group consultants came. I personally found the meeting indispensable for staying engaged with the staff, and trying to understand not only the many problems they faced, but also as a source of clinical information, including seeing ‘the person inside the psychosis’ which otherwise would have been denied me.

Dr Peter Agulnik FRCPsych

London

Sarah Jackson  

This little volume is the third in the Society of Analytical Psychology Monograph Series. It is aimed, as are the earlier two publications, at trainees and recently qualified psychotherapists and psychodynamic counsellors, although I believe it also has something to offer more experienced practitioners. Written by a Jungian analyst who originally trained as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist before further training at the SAP, it covers key theories in Jungian analytic and psychoanalytic thinking, presented from an integrated viewpoint and as taught in major Jungian trainings today. The author explains the theoretical concepts of the ego and the self, and of individuation. In describing the ultimate goal of individuation, Jung wrote that it was ‘important only as an idea; the essential thing is the opus which leads to the goal; that is the goal of a lifetime’ (Jung 1946, p. 200, italics in original). In firmly locating clinical work as central throughout this book, Clark describes the evolution and development of these concepts and theories, and their place in current post-Jungian and psychoanalytic thinking. She then illustrates this with a series of case histories and clinical examples which bring the theory to life. Her point, that it is the relation ‘between the ego and the self in the work that makes us take the self seriously’ (p. xviii), also helps to put the work in context. It is the working relationship between the ego and self of the therapist and of the patient that is of such value in depth psychology. Including more of the self in consciousness is the task of analysis, work which in the process of individuation is never completed.

The arrangement of this book is compact and it is easy to use as a quick reference. It is divided into sections covering well-structured short explanations of complex theoretical concepts.

Aging & Mental Health10(6), 574-582, 2006

Age, Gender, and the Under-Utilization of Mental Health Services: The Influence of Help-Seeking Attitudes

C.S. Mackenzie, W.L. Gekosk and V.J. Knox

The objectives of this study were to explore age and gender differences in attitudes toward seeking professional psychological help, and to examine whether attitudes negatively influence intentions to seek help among older adults and men, whose mental health needs are underserved. To achieve these objectives 206 community-dwelling adults completed questionnaires measuring help-seeking attitudes, psychiatric symptomatology, prior help-seeking, and intentions to seek help. Older age and female gender were associated with more positive help-seeking attitudes in this sample, although age and gender interacted with marital status and education, and had varying influences on different attitude components. Age and gender also influenced intentions to seek professional psychological help. Women exhibited more favourable intentions to seek help from mental health professionals than men, likely due to their positive attitudes concerning psychological openness. Older adults exhibited more favourable intentions to seek help from primary care physicians than younger adults, a finding that was not explained by age differences in attitudes. Results from this study suggest that negative attitudes related to psychological openness might contribute to men's under-utilization of mental health services. Help-seeking attitudes do not appear to be a barrier to seeking professional help among older adults, although their intentions to visit primary care physicians might be. These findings suggest the need for education to improve men's help-seeking attitudes and to enhance older adults' willingness to seek specialty mental health services.



Aging & Mental Health10(6), 638-647, 2006

Giving up or Finding a Solution? The Experience of Attempted Suicide in Later Life

L. Crocker, L. Clare and K. Evans

Older people constitute one of the highest risk groups for suicide. Existing research in this area has been largely dominated by a risk factor approach. This is of limited usefulness since only a minority of those at risk go on to make an attempt. Therefore, prediction, prevention and the management of risk remain challenging. The present study aimed to capture the subjective experience of older people who had recently made a suicide attempt, through exploring their understanding of the pathway to and from this attempt, within the context of ageing. Fifteen participants were interviewed. Transcripts were analysed using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis. Three broad themes emerged - Struggle (experiencing life as a struggle before and after the attempt, and in relation to growing older), Control (trying to maintain control over life before the attempt, and following it either failing or succeeding to regain control) and Visibility (feeling invisible or disconnected from others and trying to fight against this before the attempt and either becoming more or less connected afterwards). Risk factors identified in the literature were often absent or construed by participants as not relevant to their attempt. Individual accounts highlight the diversity and complexity of experience of older people who attempt suicide.

Editorial

Linda Pethick and Liane Aukin

Liane Aukin

[linda@bpethick.freeserve.co.uk]

[laukin@btinternet.com]

Liane Aukin  

Our psychoanalytical past and present are both strongly represented in this issue of the BJP. An important part of our history is given a fresh view in two strong papers from the recent Freud-Jung Letters Conference, followed by a third review essay of the recently published correspondence between Jung and Fr. Victor White. Other contemporary subjects include a paper on research, aspects of Kleinian theory, assessment in supervision and a plea for mothers with certain pathologies to be treated jointly with their babies.

We begin with the papers of James Astor and James Fisher who, from different perspectives, describe the development of the relationship between Freud and Jung and its sad ending as revealed so vividly in the letters between them. These extended papers cover the same material but they understand and interpret in very different ways the intensity of the bond between the two men and the emotional drama of their situation. James Astor corrects the traditional Freudocentric view of the relationship and tells the story of the beginning and middle phase of their relationship and their final falling out in a fluent and dramatic way; James Fisher links the story to these two remarkable men's developing thoughts on psychosis, and brings in the parallel with King Lear in Freud's ambivalence to finding a successor to carry forward and develop his ideas. There is much else that can be drawn from these letters, not least their inspiring struggle to get to the truth of mental life. It is also salutary to think again about the beginnings of the profession and what we can learn from our history.

In our next paper we turn from the beginnings of psychoanalysis to contemporary Kleinian theory. ‘A Kleinian theory of sexuality’ by Trevor Lubbe spells out the development of Freud's theories in Klein and then uses Meltzer's development of Klein to refute André Green's well-publicized view that Freud's theories have been desexualized, in particular by British Object Relations theorists.

Isabel Menzies Lyth 1917-2008

Reflections by Lou Corner, Bob Hinshelwood, Peter Agulnik, Denis Flynn, Anna Motz, Estela Welldon, Jean E. Neumann and Monica Lanyado

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

Ann Scott  

Isabel Menzies Lyth was ‘that rare combination, a distinguished psychoanalyst and social scientist’ (Barnett 2008), and ‘a formidable consultant in Tavistock group relations conferences’ (Dartington 2008) with a ‘deep respect for the psychotic processes in groups’ and for the need ‘to remain open to their study without being blown off course by them’ (The Times 2008). She may always be best known for ‘The functioning of social systems as a defence against anxiety’ (Menzies 1959), but it was a combined concern with the social, the organizational and the individual that ran through her life, and sustained her both professionally and personally. I remember this well in her, as her editor in the 1980s, and later as a friend. In compiling this tribute, I simply sought memories of her impact, professionally and personally.1 A tireless devotion to life and development characterized Isabel, and the reflections here illustrate it in the different strands of her life.

Ann Scott

1Full accounts of Isabel Menzies Lyth's life can be found in the obituaries by Lynn Barnett and Tim Dartington, and by myself in The Times, which can be accessed online.522

Ann Scott and Hilary Dewing

Hilary Dewing

annscott33@aol.com

hilary.dewing@btinternet.com

Hilary Dewing  

The question of an analytic stance, and how it can be understood across a range of registers, is the explicit and implicit theme of this issue of the BJP.

Within our profession, governance is usually discussed as a matter - sometimes contentious - of impending statutory registration. Within a political register, a requirement to make the interests of the public paramount is central, but poses difficult questions about reconciling such a requirement with the privacy and individuality of the analytic treatment. Ann Casement has a particular interest in comparative aspects of this debate, and brings her wealth of experience, internationally and as a former Chair of the United Kingdom Council for Psychotherapy, to the discussion. Her focus, wide-ranging and contextualizing, is on the way in which legal process in the round relates to the mental health field in the UK. Noting that ‘transparency and accountability are the twin pillars of ethical governance not only in the mental health field but in the socio-political-economic life of much of today's world’, she suggests that they are ‘particularly vital in the kinds of small, face-to-face organizations that abound in the analytical and psychotherapy world’. She further argues that ‘ethical governance in psychotherapy and psychoanalytic organizations is imperative in order to support the inner ethical needs as well as the ethical practice of psychotherapists and psychoanalysts in their consulting rooms’. In an informative and robustly thought-provoking contribution, Casement identifies the implications of recent legislation for the psychotherapy professions. She traces the origin of the Psychological Professions Alliance Group (which includes the UKCP and the British Psychoanalytic Council), and identifies its current work with the Head of Professional Regulation at the Department of Health in London. Perhaps most controversial - and doubtless a focus of ongoing debate - will be the idea of National Occupational Standards for Psychotherapy, currently being developed under the auspices of one of the UK sector skills councils, Skills for Health.

James Fisher

James Fisher

[jvfisher@btinternet.com]

James Fisher  

psychoses, dementia praecox, ‘heriting’, King Lear, Sigmund Freud, C.G. Jung, Emma Jung

This paper explores one dimension of the complex relationship linking Freud and Jung as revealed in their correspondence between 1906 and 1912. It focuses on Freud's adoption of Jung as his heir, particularly in terms of his repeated proposal to Jung ‘to continue and complete my work by applying to psychoses what I have begun with neuroses’. The paper tracks the fate of this proposal in the words of these two men and suggests that the ambivalence of both can be seen as an expression of an unconscious dynamic portrayed in Shakespeare's King Lear, a dynamic characterized by the author as the developmental task of ‘heriting’. Emma Jung captured the heart of the dilemma of ‘heriting’ in her question to Freud: ‘Doesn't one often give much because one wants to keep much?’ Although the trajectory of the heritage Freud sought for his ‘adopted eldest son’, ‘crown prince’ and ‘successor’ was not the same as that of the tragedy of Lear, it was no less poignant in its tensions and disappointments - even for a time in its reversal of the ‘heriting’ - and finally in the disintegration of the relationship.

This edition contains papers which reflect the breadth of ideas of interest to BJP readers - diversity, working with perversions, issues of race, psychotherapy training, observation, and language. At the heart of these papers is, as Lowe reminds us, Strachey's view (1934) that ‘a true transference interpretation is one which the analyst most fears and most wishes to avoid, as there is something about truth that is disturbing and that it is important to stay calm in the face of the anxieties which surround it’.

Following Steven Mendoza's paper in BJP 23.3 we are pleased to have further papers from the LCP's series of lectures on ‘Diversity’. Farhad Dalal, Frank Lowe and Helen Morgan's papers, all adapted from papers given at those lectures, each think about issues of race. In his paper, ‘Against the celebration of diversity’, Dalal takes a sweeping view, incorporating sociological and philosophical ideas. He notes the way that liberalism achieves a sense of equality by stripping persons of all their particularities - gender, ethnicity, status, and so on - in the process making the individual that liberalism addresses universal - ‘It is an everybody and anybody’. He points out that, although liberalism deliberately blinds itself to differences of ‘kind’ in order not to favour one individual over another because of some status differential, the results are less positive. Yet he also observes that a sense of identity as something unitary is in fact illusory, ‘Each of us is simultaneously a part of a great many cultures - the ethos of one often in conflict with that of another. If cultures are conflictual and divided, then so are the individuals that both inhabit and constitute them’. He concludes his fascinating paper by highlighting the idea that the themes of inclusion and exclusion are integral to the sense of self.

Frank Lowe's paper, ‘Colonial object relations: going underground black- white relationships’, addresses in both a careful and lively fashion the way that we can each form within us what he calls ‘colonial object relations’.

Harold Bourne  

In New Zealand, some 26 years after wearing Freud's dinner jacket, Dr Z became my patient. It was two more years before I learnt of this historic distinction of his - years which involved nerve-wracking experiences for both of us. One was my becoming the butt of medical faculty atrocity stories about psychoanalysis; another culminated in public embarrassment set up for me in a vengeful moment by Anna Freud. In this period, too, it came about that Dr Z had two close encounters with death.

My daughter Penelope, then at university, initiated this sequence. While she is now a lawyer, at that time she was studying Russian and given to blaming me for her predicament with her professor, Dr Z. Somehow, she had become a favoured student, uncomfortably privileged with special tutorials (alongside a shaggy and smelly dog) and, her father being a fellow academic, faced with expectations in Russian beyond any good sense. Partly this was because Dr Z was too foreign and off-beat to engage most other students, but doubtless all this was symptomatic as well of his mind being obstinately cast in St Petersburg and Vienna, despite having fled Europe years before and found refuge here within striking distance of the South Pole.

Suddenly, we had an emergency. Dr Z had some Russian literature research project in hand which, Penelope supposed, had to be crazy because he needed her father's psychiatric expertise to assist with it. Unless I gave him whatever enlightenment he required forthwith, her Russian exam results would be a fiasco. It was all up to me now and, prudently, she had already attributed to me a penchant for the obscurities of poets and literary creation, which had enticed him even more. Thus flattered and manipulated, I acceded to a paternal duty to seduce Dr Z into amiable collegiality with myself and hence promote leniency towards Penelope's faltering Russian.

Read together these two books provide an excellent opportunity to catch up with the changing landscape of psychoanalytic theory. The authors/editors of each summarize attachment theory and related empirical research, and then place it alongside intersubjective approaches and, most importantly, illustrate its use in psychoanalytic practice.

The magnitude of recent changes in psychoanalytic thinking is not easily exaggerated. Peter Fonagy states that, ‘Only in the last decade and a half, as the psychoanalytic mainstream appeared to almost have evaporated in the United States, have the contributions of the interpersonalist tradition come to be acknowledged’ (Fonagy 2001, p. 125). Although both these volumes address issues relevant to these developments, they differ widely in their structure and their objectives.

Attachment and Intersubjectivity is a co-authored text that offers a clear and careful argument for the place of attachment theory as an intersubjective model within the psychoanalytic cannon. Diamond and Marrone acknowledge that the proportion of psychoanalysts who appreciate Bowlby's contribution is still small but argue that it is increasing. Nicola Diamond is Director of the PhD Programme at the School of Psychotherapy and Counselling, Regent's College, London, and she also teaches for the Open University. The clarity of her exposition may reflect her experience as a teacher. Mario Marrone, author/editor of both books, is a practising psychoanalyst and group analyst.

Attachment Theory and the Psychoanalytic Process is an edited volume which demonstrates that clinicians in Britain, Europe, the United States and Latin America are beginning to use attachment theory and related empirical research creatively to examine clinical issues. Its co-editor, Mauricio Cortina, is Director of the Attachment and Human Development Center at the Institute of Contemporary Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis in Washington, DC, and Psychoanalytic Member of the Instituto de Sociopsicoanálisis, A.C. Mexico City.

The Presence of the Therapist: Treating Childhood Trauma by Monica Lanyado. Published by Brunner-Routledge, Hove, 2004.

Peter Wilson

Peter Wilson

London

Peter Wilson  

This book is a delight. Delight? How can this be? An odd word to describe a book filled with clinical accounts of children who have experienced appalling trauma - a 10 year-old boy raised by a mentally ill mother whose love for him was periodically shattered by her outbursts of violence; a previously happy and well-balanced 9 year-old girl who had suddenly been gagged and raped by a stranger; a 9 year-old boy who had witnessed his father murder his mother when he was aged 2; a 10 year-old boy who had been subjected to a perverse incestuous relationship with his father from the age of 3 to 8. There are others too, less extreme though deeply troubled, having lost their natural parents and in transition from foster care to adoption.

There is in fact in these clinical stories little of delight. These are children who have been terrified, tormented and tortured - they show none of the spontaneity and joy of growing up, no matter how resilient they may prove to be. And those who care for them can share none of the laughter and hope that parents of non-traumatized children can cherish and enjoy. There is here no pleasure, no charm, and no room for sentimentality.

So where is the delight? The delight resides in the presence of the therapist, Monica Lanyado, the author of this book. At the heart of this book is a woman who fundamentally believes in the potential in all of us - no matter how devastated - to grow, to develop, to find some new opportunity or pathway that can to some degree rectify or change the damage of the past. This is not a naïve belief, for she in no way hides from the fact that all of us carry a dark side that, if exposed, can be foul, perverse and profoundly destructive.

In her accounts of her work as a child psychotherapist, she writes clearly and lucidly of the, at times, awful behaviour of children towards her and of the full gamut of feelings aroused in her. Children who have been disturbed by the abuse inflicted on them invariably turn round in any relationship likely to become intimate and make the other go through the very experiences that they have endured. There is no doubt that Lanyado in her therapeutic work has well and truly been there - at the butt end of the extremities of the brutal and soul-destroying projections of these children. She has allowed herself to feel something of what it feels like to be as traumatized as these children have been.

The Prenatal Theme in Psychotherapy by Philippe Ployé. Published by Karnac, London, 2006; 143 pp; £19.99 paperback.

Margaret Cohen

Margaret Cohen

[magfcoh@blueyonder.co.uk]

Margaret Cohen  

It seems that as humans we have always thought of our existence as set within its confines. So we think of death and what this means for our existence, but also of birth. And this leads us to imagine what our prebirth existence is like and what birth means for us. Philippe Ployé's book The Prenatal Theme in Psychotherapy is full of thoughts about our perinatal and prenatal life. He raises questions about the possibility of object-directed prenatal forms of relatedness and of prenatal forms of aggression. Then we wonder what this aggression could be directed towards, and he suggests the prenatal mother herself and the placenta.

I found Ployé's writing stimulating in terms of making me think more imaginatively about prenatal life and, more specifically, about the placenta. I came to feel that I had badly overlooked the importance of this vital organ, although I had been aware of Meltzer talking of it as the baby's first companion. Ployé makes the placenta vivid with his list of placental symbols, but much more through his keen awareness of the service that the placenta provides for the baby. He makes one want to know more about the mechanism of the placental membrane. He cites E.W. Page as describing this membrane as ‘highly dynamic’ and both separating and linking the foetus and the mother. Page says that it receives input from both and is believed to play an active role in ‘determining the nature of these exchanges as well as the rate at which they occur’ (Ployé, p. 123; Page 1963, p. 147). Ployé places great importance on this ‘dual-touch’ interchange and sees it as the physical forerunner of Bion's container/contained and of Kleinian ideas of projective identification and projection. He points out that, in describing these, we often talk about ‘metabolizing’, and that when we talk about the physical processes by which the placenta receives the wastes of the baby and provides him with oxygen and nutrients, we use the word ‘metabolizing’ unmetaphorically.

This raises for him the question of the placenta as a transference object. He cites Sydney Klein (1984) who used the idea of the placenta as a transference object in a psychotherapy case. In the elaboration of his case, Dr Klein sees his patient as reacting to a cold heartless breast with a foetal regression. He has an idea that in reality his patient's mother was distant to her son in infancy and sexually seductive later. Dr Klein thinks of the patient in the transference as then seeking a placental object ‘which fitted him perfectly at all points’ (1984, p. 312). Immediately, bad things are taken away without negotiation, where there is no time and little gravity.

John Woods

John Woods

London
[jwoods@tavi-port.nhs.uk]

John Woods  

I first approached this book out of a personal rather than a professional interest, since as a psychotherapist I have never considered myself as specializing in ‘psychosomatic’ problems. Rather instead I have been exploring over the years the psychological and emotional dimensions of mainly behavioural problems. However, this book has made me re-think much of my professional as well as personal experience. Addressed as it is to a wider audience than that of psychotherapy, it nevertheless utilizes the knowledge that we perhaps take for granted and delves deeper into its implications.

The book is full of clinical anecdotes as well as fully documented research, some of it well established, and some much more recent. Much of the research goes to show the complex link between mind and body and that the psyche is crucial to the correct diagnosis and understanding of physical ailments. At the risk of oversimplifying the varied information contained in the book, I would like to pick one very basic connection the authors point to, which is the significance of change. The authors quote many studies that repeatedly show how important life events precede major illnesses and disorders. The list of such findings goes on and on, so that more than any other predisposing factor it ‘… is change that predicts illness’ (p. 60). But it is precisely these life changes and their emotional impact that are ignored in conventional medical practice.

The authors seek to attack certain fundamental assumptions that exist in conventional medical thinking. The ‘scientific’ approach seeks to isolate a specific cause, and to locate that cause of illness as an external influence on the body. This is referred to as the ‘infection model’, i.e. that a certain bacteria (or the equivalent) is responsible for the illness and its symptoms. The starting point of many of their observations is the limited perspective that any diagnostician such as a GP might have in hearing about and understanding an illness. It is the difference between saying ‘I have had this symptom for three months’ and ‘the symptoms started when my wife left me three months ago’. The book produces a wealth of experimental evidence as to the importance of such connections between mind and body. In one experiment holes were punched in the roofs of the mouths of a group of dental students, once during a vacation period and once just before exam time. A wound in the same individual took an average of 40% longer to heal at around exam time stress. The authors point out that, if exam time stress can have such an effect on wound healing, we must also imagine the effects of long-term chronic human misery.

Linda Pethick  

This short book is an expanded version of a series of six lectures given by Neville Symington in Australia during 2004. The lecture series asked the question: ‘How is it that someone who has a problem is able to resolve it through conversation with another?’ The question posed is not: ‘Can someone who has a problem resolve it through conversation with another?’ This question is tackled briefly in a section on whether it is possible to change in later life or whether only the early mother can have an effect on development, but mostly that question is presumed to have been answered in the affirmative, thus what is pondered throughout the book is how and why it is that psychotherapy works, the ‘how healing happens’ of the subtitle.

The fact that this was originally a series of lectures contains both its strength and its weakness. As always with Symington there are fascinating asides and quotations and linked thoughts, making it easy to pick up the book and read just a few lines or pages and get something from it, and read in this way it is most enjoyable.

London

Diana Birkett  

Hanna Segal is widely regarded as the chief exponent of Kleinian thought in this country, and one of the clearest exponents of Bion's early work. This book includes both expositions of Klein's and Bion's ideas, and new contributions of Segal's own, on the subjects of dream theory, disillusionment, vision, and September 11th (Papers from 2000-2006).

In the two interviews which conclude the book, we get a lively sense of what motivated the young Polish student on her arrival here in 1939. She met Fairbairn while pursuing her medical studies in Edinburgh, and he gave her two books to read: Anna Freud's The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence, and Klein's The Psychoanalysis of Children. Her choice was clear: on applying to the Institute, she insisted on waiting until Klein had a vacancy for a training analysis, despite being offered a place with Winnicott. Much can be deduced from these beginnings: the interviews reveal a strong polemical streak in arguing the case against Lacan, some aspects of feminism, and revisionist theories of homosexuality.

In the first of these papers (‘Interpretation of dreams - 100 years on’), delivered in Vienna on the centenary of Freud's famous work, she makes what I think is one of her most original contributions to classical psychoanalytic theory - characteristically by paying tribute to her eminent predecessor, but introducing a significant variation on the original theory. She holds that ‘a central part of dream work is to evolve a symbolic language’ (p. 16), and that this is a function of the ego - not necessarily for the purpose of wish-fulfilment but as a reparative endeavour in the internal world - an attempt to restore destroyed objects and aspects of oneself (p. 24). This hints at a further theme, developed later on in the book: that this struggle for representation in dreams is in the service of the reality-principle, and involves mourning and loss, rather than a gratification of the pleasure-principle.

Jung's ‘White Raven’

The Jung-White Letters edited by Ann Conrad Lammers and Adrian Cunningham, Consulting Editor Murray Stein. Published by Routledge, London and New York, 2007; 384 pp; £50.00 hardback.

Christopher MacKenna

Christopher MacKenna

London
[cmackenna@stmarylebone.org]

Christopher MacKenna  

The publication of the letters between Carl Jung and Fr Victor White, the English Dominican theologian and psychotherapist, is a major landmark in Jungian studies. It has also been a long time in coming. But at last we have them, and in a beautifully produced and meticulously edited edition, supplied with copious footnotes and six appendices which provide much background and contextual information. Ann Conrad Lammers, Adrian Cunningham, and Murray Stein deserve the warmest congratulations and thanks for their devoted and scholarly labour of love in finally bringing The Jung-White Letters to print.

By a happy coincidence, 2007 also saw the publication of the first book-length biography of Victor White: Fr. Victor White, O.P.: The Story of Jung's ‘White Raven’ (Weldon 2007). Readers of The Letters who wish to know more about this remarkable priest, whose sometimes impassioned discussions and arguments with Jung helped to inspire - or, maybe, to provoke - Jung's works Aion (1968) and Answer to Job (1969), will appreciate this authoritative exposition of White's personal and intellectual development. Together, The Letters and Weldon's biography of White greatly enrich the picture painted by Ann Conrad Lammers in her earlier study, In God's Shadow: The Collaboration of Victor White and C.G. Jung (Lammers 1994).

Why might we want to read these letters? Most obviously, I guess, if we are interested in the dialogue between Jungian psychology and Christianity; or if we are seeking another entrée into the many-faceted character of Jung. But to say this is to give no inkling of the richness of these pages.

The Protagonists

As his semi-autobiographical memoir, Memories, Dreams, Reflections (Jung 1963), revealed, Jung - a clergyman's son - was preoccupied, from the time of his lonely childhood, with the problems raised by religion; but it was only when he was in his 70s, meeting Victor White, that he encountered a theological soul-mate who was able to understand his psychological point of view.

Introduction: Why Spirituality?

Lesley Murdin

Lesley Murdin

[Lesley.Murdin@wpf.org.uk]

Lesley Murdin  

Analytic psychotherapy can have many aims and one of the outcomes that it aims to achieve is to enable the patient to establish his own personal morals and perhaps his own relationship with the eternal and transcendental truths to which we may aspire even though they remain for ever out of reach.

WPF is particularly concerned with this area of human experience and has been since its foundation in 1969 by the Revd William Kyle, a Methodist minister, who set up a clinical service and training to help his clergy who were running into difficulties in advising and counselling their parishioners without having had any serious training to help them. In particular he wanted to help them set appropriate boundaries. To do this, he enlisted the help of a group of supervisors and trainers who were analysts and analytical psychologists from the Institute of Psychoanalysis and the Society of Analytical Psychology. In keeping with this tradition, and as part of an analytic therapeutic training lasting about seven years on average, WPF offers a module on ontology. This is the study of being or what constitutes the subject. Each developing psychotherapist examines assumptions about politics, gender, philosophy, sociology and religion. Each candidate in training is asked to discover the contributory elements of his or her sense of self: the construction of the I.

As part of this endeavour, WPF organized a conference on the theme of ‘The Forgotten Fountain’ in September 2007. This fountain is perhaps the spring that provides life to each individual and may have a numinous quality to it, or it may be something purely mundane and more closely physiological like the life-force. With a definition as broad as this, no one can be left out since a certain commitment to the life-force is needed to set a human being going and it is the source of the energy that compels us to keep asking questions of ourselves and others. An interest in spirituality may perhaps be thought of as an interest in a search for something beyond everyday experience or maybe only as a desire to articulate the existential questions that need to be raised; Professor Andrew Samuels defined the spiritual realm at a recent WPF conference as ‘beyond the personal’ (Samuels 2008).

Isabel Menzies Lyth 1917-2008

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood   Fellow, British Psychoanalytical Society; Professor of Psychoanalytic Studies, University of Essex

Isabel Menzies was my first supervisor in my training to be a psychoanalyst. One of my most vivid memories was of one weekly supervision, in 1975, when she had a rather ostentatious posture with her hand draped on the back of the couch she sat on. Very visible was an engagement ring. Being a timid trainee I did not enquire about it, but it transpired that she was retiring from the Tavistock to get married to Oliver Lyth and move to him in Oxford. It was a very romantic little drama. Romance and ostentation are not qualities that really describe Isabel, who was a very down-to-earth Scots woman, who had originally trained as an economist and had found her way - through the work of the Tavistock Institute - to psychoanalysis.

I owe a lot to Isabel, and remarks she made in my supervision with her still come back to me as guiding lights that illuminate many problems in clinical work. One I always remember was her dismissal of what she called the ‘you mean me’ style of interpreting the transference, and it has always been a creative challenge to develop more meaningful, and less formulaic, interpretations which can live in the moment rather than distance analyst and analysand from the moment.

Anna Motz   Consultant Clinical and Forensic Psychologist, Oxford Secure Services; Past President, International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy

When I started as a nursing assistant on the McKnight Unit in Oxford in 1987, having just graduated with a degree in psychology and philosophy, I was totally new to psychiatry and had not encountered profound mental illness before. One of the most surprising aspects of the work was the weekly staff group, where we gathered for one hour, with an invited guest, the facilitator of the group, Isabel Menzies Lyth. I had no idea who this elegant elderly woman who arrived on the dot of one, and marched out on the dot of two, regardless of whether anyone was still speaking, was, or what her function in the group could be, but it gradually became evident that she had clear, strong views about what was going on organizationally and interpersonally in the ward, and had no compunction about making her observations public.

Meg Williams

Meg Williams

[www.artlit.info]

Meg Williams  

This is an avowedly idiosyncratic work that refuses to dumb down Bion's ideas or regularize them to suit established preconceptions. It is steeped in the author's long apprenticeship to Bion and his works, which began - he tells us - in the 1970s when, as an analysand of Bion's, he first became enthralled by his ideas. In line with this seminal identification, Grotstein takes fast hold of Bion's Platonic emphasis on ‘becoming’ and invites us to participate in his current phase of ‘digestion’ of Bion as a life-changing phenomenon. From this vertex his book could perhaps have been subtitled ‘Wilfred Bion's legacy to an analysand’. It is not intended to be a summary of the Bionic canon but, rather, a model for immersion in Bionic turbulence. Much of its vitality derives from the author's personal wrestling with the concepts, and he states frankly that, even after years of study, the conclusions presented here are still ‘tentative in my mind’:

This is one of the rewards and joys of ‘dreaming’ - that is, absorbing and transforming - Bion's works and maintaining the personal faith, not that I would understand Bion and his works, but that I would become as much of the wisdom, O, of his works as my mind can possibly progressively accommodate. (p. 329)

When confronted by a thinker of Bion's magnitude, who ‘disturbs the universe’ of our existing mentality, we are invited into regions where ‘most of us absolutely cannot follow’ (Meltzer 1997, p. 63). We cannot develop his ideas, but we can develop ourselves through internal review and consolidation in response to them. Meltzer advised:

It seemed to me that the way to enjoy Bion was very much what he himself had advised: just read it; don't try to understand it, don't try to figure it out; just read it, enjoy it and if you are lucky you will be inspired by it. (Meltzer 1997, p. 65)

Grotstein's book makes Bion very real in the sense that we experience the impact of Bion's ideas on his thinking: that is, not just his dogma or allegiance but his inner being and becoming, a process he calls ‘incarnation of godhead’ or ‘godhood’ - which, in traditional Kleinian terms, would surely be introjection of the object in its dual capacity to both feed the internal baby and advance its capacity for mental digestion. Or, in traditional poetic terms, this is what is meant by ‘inspiration’ by the Muse.

James Astor

James Astor

[james.astor@btinternet.com]

James Astor  

Dear Editors

I have read Tim Martin's interesting paper (BJP 24(2): 184-96) and am concerned that it could give the impression that Freud regularly made use of his sculpture collection as part of his analytic practice. Martin's interest in the use HD made of Freud's sculpture is pertinent to her psychopathology but to imply that Freud made a practice of using his collection for psychotherapeutic purposes cannot, in my view, be derived from this one example.

This article claims in the title and text that Freud used sculpture in his analytic practice. This gives the impression that Freud regularly made use of these artefacts as part of a psychotherapeutic process. However, Martin acknowledges that Freud ‘never claimed that his sculptures were a direct part of his clinical practice’. He further states that there are a number of accounts of Freud using sculpture in analysis, although what ‘using sculpture in analysis’ means is not clear. As far as I could tell Martin bases his assertion on the fact that as the sculptures were on display in Freud's apartment this suggests that ‘they were an active part of the clinical process’. The question here might be clinical process for whom? It is an interesting point to speculate what role these artefacts had in Freud's practice and how they affected his patients. Clinicians recognize that their consulting room and its contents have emotional significance for their patients but Martin is suggesting that there was an intentional display of artefacts by Freud as an active part of the treatment process. Martin's account records that HD did not ‘notice Freud's presence’ when she came to her first appointment but looked at the objects in his apartment. She appeared to be dissociated and by using one of the objects in his collection Freud was able to make a connection to her. HD records this. Clearly for HD these sculptures were a significant part of her clinical experience. The issue is did the way Freud use the Athena sculpture with HD indicate that he used his collection as an active therapeutic part of his work with other patients? It must be significant that Freud never published any account of an analysis which implied that using sculpture was part of his practice.

Correction

Paul Williams

Paul Williams

[pw@pwilliams.eu]

Paul Williams  

Dear Editors

You published an article of mine entitled ‘The worm that flies in the night’ in BJP 23(3): 343-64, 2007. It has been drawn to my attention by Dr Marta Brody that, through an incorrect citation and a failure to cite Dr Brody as the author of the ideas in a passage in this article, the work of Dr Brody has been misrepresented and wrongly attributed to Susan Deri. I now wish to correct this very unfortunate mistake, for which I take full responsibility.

In the final section of my paper in a passage on the work of Paul Klee, I write:

‘… the last piece by Paul Klee, left standing on his easel in 1940 … is considered by many to be the most monumental work of his career. The painting unites familiar objects of Klee's studio (the glass muller, the coffee-pot), images from his career (the strewn flowers, sometimes in the shape of P, also the coffee-pot) and objects that signify the void and death (notably the angel of death portrayed humorously) and crosses reminiscent of earlier work at the time of his mother's death (Deri 1984). Klee, in poor health, had been occupied by concerns about death for many years. Here, he demonstrates his remarkable capacity for utilizing potential space and transitional thinking, expressed through the simultaneous freedom of composition and unity of structure. He creates a symbolic bridge that unites his past and present artistic life and world and his impending death (Deri 1984).’

The ideas, words and interpretations in this paragraph were attributed to Susan Deri, whereas their legitimate author is Dr Brody. Although Dr Brody's article on Klee (‘Paul Klee: art, potential space and the transitional process’, Psychoanalytic Review 88(3): 369-92, June 2001), from which the above ideas were drawn, was cited in the references in my article, a commensurate attribution of her ideas was missing from the text. These two mistakes together gave rise both to misattribution and a potential misunderstanding that Dr Brody's ideas could have derived from Deri, a situation that would be wholly incorrect. I apologize to Dr Brody for this error and for any distress it has caused her.

From Cabinet to Couch: Freud's Clinical Use of Sculpture

Tim Martin PHD

Tim Martin

418 Aylestone Road, Leicester LE2 8JA. [tdmartin@dmu.ac.uk]

Tim Martin  

Freud, sculpture, Hilda Doolittle, H.D., clinical setting

This article aims to address and remedy the fact that Freud's clinical use of sculpture has received little sustained attention. After a brief review of the collection, Melanie Klein's clinical use of dolls is discussed as an initial basis for comparison. It then makes a detailed examination of primary evidence found in the published writings and private correspondence of the writer and analysand H.D. (Hilda Doolittle). H.D.'s analysis indicates that Freud used sculpture as an analogue for the ‘foreign body’ of psychical trauma, treating it as a representation of a representation, or Vorstellungrepräsentanz. The sculptures also served Freud's archaeological metaphor for the ‘otherness’ of the unconscious in ways that architectural fragments did not. The author then considers H.D.'s hallucination of Athena Nike and Freud's use of his own damaged sculpture of Athena to raise therapeutic questions about her phallic relation to the signifier in the treatment of her writer's block. This case study is further compared to Klein and to Jung in order to differentiate the use of objects in the clinical setting and to mark some of the limits Freud encountered in H.D.'s second analytic session. The author concludes that purely textual examinations of Freud may have greatly underestimated his clinical use of sculpture in recuperating lost memories as fundamental indices of desire.

The Perversion of Language in the Analyst's Activity: Navigating the Rhythms of Embodiment and Symbolization

Steven H. Knoblauch

In this short text, the problem of how ‘the talking cure’ itself can become a perverse relation is considered and illustrated with a brief clinical vignette. Contributions coming from the work of Stern in infant research and Lacan in post-Freudian thought illuminate the potential for experience to be split off through the use of language itself. These perspectives are brought to bear on thinking about representation, splitting, and perversion as a basis for considering a clinical instance in which patient and analyst enact a perverse relation constituted by the way in which the patient uses the analyst's language to construct a sado-masochistic perversion of the treatment process. Within the clinical episode, Stein's reformulation of perversion, informed by Ogden's observations and expanding Stoller's earlier contribution, provides a basis for considering how the analyst was able to use attention to the body-based countertransferential experience to repair a sense of ‘erasure’ that was being accomplished for both analyst and analysand through the enactment.



International Forum of Psychoanalysis16, 204-212, 2007

New Approaches to Understanding Unconscious Processes: Implicit and Explicit Memory Systems

Mauricio Cortina and Giovanni Liotti

Freud viewed the unconscious as being roughly equivalent to dynamically repressed wishes, needs, and motivations. Findings from developmental psychology, cognitive psychology, psychoanalysis, and neuroscience over the past 40 years have dramatically changed our views of unconscious processes and the human mind. It is now clear that Freud's dynamic unconscious is only a minor segment of information that is processed at subsymbolic, implicit, and automatic levels. Only a fraction of this information is further processed at explicit conscious levels. Moreover, the vast majority of the information that remains nonconscious is adaptive and has major consequences for development. We examine some clinical implications of these views.

On Aggression and Violence: An Analytic Perspective by Richard Mizen and Mark Morris. Published by Palgrave Macmillan, New York, 2007; 244 pp.

Alejandro Reyes

Alejandro Reyes

London

Alejandro Reyes  

This is an extremely interesting critical review of the concepts of violence and aggression as applied in psychoanalysis. It is an ambitious work that covers very difficult and uncertain ground since, in the process of tracing the origins and development of aggression and violence, it casts light on the origins of the mind in the body, the process known as mentation. It is therefore relevant well beyond the fields of forensic psychiatry and psychoanalysis in which the authors are undoubtedly deeply experienced. It is also fresh and original whilst bringing into focus and context, particularly in the chapters on transference, countertransference, violence against the self and sex and violence, most of the conceptual information indispensable to the present-day psychoanalytic therapist whether in his consulting room or other settings.

The main aim of the authors is to diversify and broaden our understanding of aggression and, in particular, to remove violence from the peculiar status in which it is often kept in psychoanalytic thinking, as somehow taken for granted as having a mindless, bodily nature. In the initial chapters the authors discuss the possible reasons why the psychoanalytical exploration of aggression and violence is relatively underdeveloped.

One reason would be the preponderance initially given by Freud to sexuality as the instinctual basis of the mind. Although in later writings he modified this position with the introduction of the death instinct, aggression continued to find an uneasy home in psychoanalytical developmental theories. It eventually resulted in a radical dissociation in the analytical movement between those who accept the existence of a primary innate aggression as fundamental to development and those who regard aggression as strictly secondary to deprivation and frustration. It is thus that the nature and origins of aggression became, in the words of the authors, a ‘totemic’ element to signal allegiance to one or other of the streams of analytical thought, so incandescent with ideological passion as to make difficult a more dispassionate, scientific attitude to the subject.

enactment, interpretation

The author discusses the vicissitudes of working analytically with patients who present with monolithic forms of thinking. He describes an approach that emphasizes the importance of the analyst as a real object that has at first to be explored to discover whether or not what is projected corresponds to the analyst's mind. This exploration of the other often confronts the analyst with their own issues surrounding sanity and madness, life and death; it is through this exploration of these real anxieties in the mind of the object that can lead to the beginnings of thinking in severely ill patients.

Engaging Imagination and the Future: Frontiers for Clinical Work

Robert N. Emde

Narrative theory indicates that assessment using narratives is expectant, collaborative, and has the potential to begin a process of change. A shift from thinking exclusively about meaning (subjectivity in the child) to thinking also about shared meaning (intersubjectivity between child and clinician-examiner) seems appropriate in the clinical context. Recent knowledge from the cognitive neurosciences makes a shift of this sort compelling and has further implications. More story stem narrative research at the level of assessing individual children needs to be done so there can be explicit links to treatment.



International Journal of Psychoanalysis88, 147-165, 2007

The PAedophile and His Inner World: Theoretical and Clinical Considerations on the Analysis of a Patient

Franco De Masi

The main feature of the treatment of the paedophile is the distance that separates the analyst from the patient. However hard the analyst tries to understand his patient, the paedophile's world appears to him, especially at the beginning of the treatment, incomprehensible, disheartening and distant. This paper describes the analytic therapy of a paedophile patient. The psychopathological organization that dominates his inner world originates from a delusional nucleus in which an object (a child or an adolescent) is idealized and worshipped in place of the parents. This object promises all manner of pleasure and happiness. The positive outcome of this patient leads one to believe that, if analytically treated, some paedophile patients are open to therapeutic transformation.



International Journal of Psychoanalysis88, 183-202, 2007

The Coming Changes in Psychoanalytic Education: Part II

Otto F. Kernberg

This paper is the second part of a general analysis of problems in contemporary psychoanalytic education. Having proposed changes in the training analysis and supervisory systems in Part I, here the author focuses on concrete proposals regarding changes in the curriculum, seminars and classroom teaching; the governance of psychoanalytic institutes, relationship of institutes with their respective psychoanalytic society and the role of the university in the development of science and research; the admission, progression, and graduating processes; certification and accreditation.
